analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and short-term rental sites to show the full price, with mandatory fees, upfront.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on April 28, 2025, with no recorded opposition; it now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires hotels, short-term rentals, and the websites that sell their rooms to display the total price — base rate plus any mandatory service fees — in every ad and from the first screen a shopper sees. It also requires disclosure of government-imposed taxes and fees before purchase. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can enforce it. Hotels and booking platforms can no longer advertise a low base rate and add mandatory fees, like resort fees, at checkout.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who books a hotel room or a short-term rental. Today, an advertised rate often excludes mandatory fees such as resort fees or cleaning fees, so the price a shopper first sees can be much lower than the price they finally pay. The bill requires the total services price — base rate plus mandatory fees — to be displayed wherever a price is shown and at every step of the buying process [S3]. Travelers can comparison-shop on the true price instead of discovering the full cost at checkout [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Travelers booking hotels and short-term rentals

how_it_helps.text: Covered entities must display the total services price — base price plus every mandatory service fee — wherever a price is shown in ads, marketing, or price lists [S3].

The total services price must be disclosed when a purchaser first sees the offering and at every later step of the buying process, and government-imposed taxes and fees must be disclosed before the final purchase [S3].
The rule covers hotels, short-term rentals, third-party online sellers, and metasearch and price-comparison platforms, so the full price follows travelers across booking sites [S3].
The FTC can enforce it as an unfair or deceptive practice, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents, giving travelers enforcement muscle beyond their own lawsuits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hotels, short-term rental operators, and the online booking platforms and metasearch sites that sell their rooms. They can no longer advertise a bare base rate while tacking mandatory fees on later, and they face FTC and state AG enforcement if they do [S3]. The bill takes effect 450 days after enactment, giving the industry time to adjust its systems [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels, rental operators, and booking platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state and local rules on price advertising unless the state rule already requires the full total services price, so a state could not impose fee-disclosure requirements stricter than the federal standard [S3].
Only the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce it — there is no private right of action for travelers who were shown a misleading price [S3].
The prohibition does not take effect until 450 days after enactment, so current pricing practices continue in the meantime [S3].

Optional charges a buyer can decline are excluded from the required total price, and booking platforms get an affirmative defense if they relied in good faith on inaccurate price data supplied by the hotel or rental host [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to travelers is real and practical: the price you compare is the price you pay, instead of mandatory fees appearing late in checkout. The costs fall on the lodging industry, whose core objection — that they may have to change how they advertise — is precisely the point of the bill. The genuine weaknesses are structural: enforcement runs only through the FTC and state AGs, state rules stricter than the federal standard are preempted, and the 450-day delay means nothing changes for over a year. On balance a well-aimed, modest consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure that requires a two-thirds majority and skips a recorded roll call, and the Senate has received it and placed it on its calendar but has not voted.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 21, 2025, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
The committee ordered the bill reported by voice vote on April 8, 2025, and formally reported it on April 24 with House Report 119-71, placing it on the Union Calendar [S5].
On April 28, 2025, the House passed the bill by voice vote on a motion to suspend the rules and pass — a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority [S5].
The Senate received the bill on April 29, 2025, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 60, where it awaits further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained the bill's protection — hotels and booking sites can keep advertising base prices with fees added later until the Senate acts and any law takes effect 450 days after enactment [S3][S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, hotel guests are no better off

sides.party_line_note: The bill cleared committee and the House by voice vote with a bipartisan sponsor-cosponsor group (a Republican sponsor, 4 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors), and no recorded opposition appears anywhere in the action history [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill ends the practice of advertising a low base rate while mandatory fees such as resort or cleaning fees appear later in checkout, and makes violations subject to FTC and state AG action. Travelers gain the true price upfront; the industry loses a marketing practice that made its advertised rates look cheaper than they were [S3].

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and metasearch platforms
industries.note: Booking and comparison platforms must show total prices across their listings, including on metasearch referrals. But they receive an affirmative defense if they relied in good faith on inaccurate price data supplied by hotels or hosts, which softens their exposure compared to the lodging operators themselves [S3].

The bill preempts state and local price-advertising rules that do not already require the full total services price, replacing a patchwork of state fee-disclosure laws with a single federal floor. States keep authority over contracts, torts, and fraud [S3].

analysis.trajectory: The bill is on the Senate calendar with no recorded opposition and bipartisan support, which usually puts a noncontroversial bill in position for expedited Senate passage — but a calendar listing guarantees nothing, and many bills die there each Congress when leaders never schedule the time. Senate action or a companion bill introduced in the Senate would tell you which way it is heading.
